meaning: The time from the player realizing they failed until they regain control; interest cools fast inside it.
Sakurai's frame-counting method: clap seconds with an in-between beat, giving about 30 frames per beat and 15 per half beat at 60 fps.
His method for feeling frames: each beat is about 30 frames at 60 fps and half a beat about 15.

term: A fight between live action and animation
meaning: What a cast or world looks like when realistic and cartoony designs are dropped together unadjusted; his shorthand for a failure of style unification.
Playing a game completely blind, 'as if I'm the first person walking on freshly-fallen snow', with no trailers, guides or Let's Plays; his preferred way to study others' work.
The time the player has control. Sakurai tracks how long the player is in control, how long not, and how much is emptiness.
Adding an element's colors to the background so the result moves toward white; distinct from translucency, which moves toward the element's own colors. Useful but not enough on its own.
The way distant things lose contrast and saturation and take on atmospheric color; used to push backdrops back and to make big things read as big.
Roger Caillois's four elements of play (competition, chance, imitation, vertigo); Sakurai places game essence mainly in agon.
Kid Icarus: Uprising's two halves: a rail-shooter flight to each battlefield (Pit's Power of Flight lasts five minutes) followed by third-person shooting on the ground.
Background sounds of a place, the lowest priority in his mix, kept quiet and fairly realistic but never cut to dead silence.
Rough edits made by moving and stretching storyboard art; in Sakurai's reveal pipeline, the point at which a video's structure and length are essentially set.
Combining two or more animations, such as blending a canceled attack into a walk; keep blends quick and snappy.
Sakurai's written document listing every animation with a text description, its length and when the attack occurs; loops are marked 'Loop' or 'Any'.
How Smash is described relative to fighting games. Sakurai stresses it is not a rejection: he admires their push and pull but felt combos removed it after the first hit.
How Sakurai frames every project: a game made to fit a given genre or goal, not a game made for his own taste.
The part of an attack animation when it can register as a hit, plus a little motion around it; hit stop freezes it into a firm, readable pose.
The opening of a sound's waveform as it rises to its peak; for impact sounds he wants it short so the sound never feels late.
One of the four values Sakurai specifies for each attack: the frame on which the attack begins to register.
The hardware rule that palettes are shared across 16x16 areas, so placing an object can recolor the ground under it.
His framing of the choice between exaggerated sounds (fiction, to sell impact) and realistic ones (non-fiction, to convey material and information).
His warning that balancing everything toward the middle makes options interchangeable and the game bland.
His target for the original Kirby: people new to games of any age or gender, as opposed to a demographic slice.
A flat object, usually a two-polygon mesh, that always faces the camera; cheap to render and ideal for particles and light flashes. A Y-axis billboard turns only around the vertical axis.
A flat object that always faces the camera; a Y-axis billboard rotates only around the vertical axis and can look too skinny when misused for effects.
Sakurai's name for the effect left behind by a sword swing, usually a fading polygon ribbon; the swing animation often has to be adjusted for it to read.
How Sakurai describes what his lessons offer: a small addition on top of your own experience, skill and way of thinking.
Sakurai's own coinage for the stop when a boss is defeated: the screen stops and flashes for a moment, used since Kirby's Adventure.

Sakurai's spec notation: each tunable value is written in plain language inside brackets with an 'O' placeholder, e.g. '[Special startup X-velocity is O]', and anything in brackets becomes a parameter.

Sakurai's spec convention: write each tunable value as a plain-language phrase in brackets with "O" as the number, e.g. [Special startup X-velocity is O]; anything inside brackets becomes a parameter.
Sakurai's spec notation: a tunable value is written as a plain-language phrase in brackets with O for the number, and anything in brackets becomes a parameter.
The point at which any player stops improving and gives up, which is why stuck players need a way forward.
How a risk that is minor to an experienced player can feel to a less experienced one.
How many kinds of players a game can reach; Sakurai holds that increasing game essence reduces it.
His habit of taking in many games and media reflectively while producing regular output (column, daily report, screenshots, the channel): 'Take a lot in, put a lot out.'
Japanese word for zooming an action figure around by hand; Sakurai suggests it as a way for animators to train an eye for poses.
Frames late in an attack's follow-through during which the player can move, jump or attack again before the animation returns to standby; added to Smash after Melee.
The usually invisible point a 3D camera looks at. Sakurai's advice: don't anchor it to the character, especially on the Y axis.
Getting gains without losses inside the game's rules, such as metal slime farming; fun and memorable, but not extended to rewriting parameters.
Kirby Air Ride's achievement grid, predating console trophies; clearing a square reveals the conditions for its neighbors.
A grid of objectives introduced in Kirby Air Ride: clearing a panel reveals the conditions of its neighbors. Later used in Smash as Challenges.
Kirby Air Ride's sandbox mode with varying power-ups and stadiums, built to widen play types rather than reward one perfect line; later the basis of Smash Run.
Bug severity classes: S for hangs or possible save corruption, A for bugs that stop progression; lower classes are sometimes waived on purpose.
Severity grades a manager assigns: Class S for hangs and bugs that might corrupt save data, Class A for bugs that stop players progressing; lower classes are sometimes waived on purpose.
Last-moment survival options, like rotating a Tetris piece after it lands, that invite greater risk-taking.
A simulation filter (now built into Photoshop) that shows how art looks with types of color blindness such as protanopia; he used it to check Meteos.
Differences in how each monitor (and room lighting) shows the same color, which he treats as fatal for art reviews.

What gives a game its appeal and direction, e.g. 'the fun of sending opponents flying'. Sakurai compares it to a lighthouse beam: keep heading toward it through any storm and never change that trajectory midway.
The step that puts edited parameter data into a build where it can be tested; one button press at Bandai Namco Studios, ten minutes plus a reboot on early Smash games.
Kirby's power to take an inhaled enemy's ability, introduced in Kirby's Adventure as an optional depth layer on top of inhale-and-spit, so every enemy gained meaning.
Polygons or simple images mixed into an effect and made its focus, giving Smash Ultimate's effects a clean, anime-style look.
Sakurai's internal daily post to his team (a screenshot plus three to five topics, open to comments), started during Brawl.
The first frame of a damage animation, held by hit stop; in Smash it's an extreme pain pose nothing like standby.
Genre control conventions (such as FPS fire and grenade buttons) that Sakurai says you're better off using, because they warm 'the handshake between human and computer'.
In-development features for testing and analyzing the game, stripped from the release build.
Sakurai's method: pick what is fun, work out why (usually risk and reward), then rebuild it into an original mechanic.
Development hardware that may run differently from the retail unit; Mushiking's was just under one square meter.
How a hand holds something swung with the forearm; a perpendicular grip makes characters look like action figures.
Delay added by a screen's picture post-processing, bypassed by Game Mode or Low Latency Mode; distinct from response time, the time a pixel takes to change color. At 60 fps, 16.67 ms is one frame.
Response time is how long a pixel takes to change color; display latency comes from picture post-processing and is what Game Mode or Low Latency Mode removes.
The draw order that decides whether characters or effects appear in front; easy to force in 2D, but forcing it in 3D causes depth disparity.
The Famicom channel that allowed sampled sounds, used sparingly early on because samples took a lot of cartridge space; Super Mario Bros. 3's timpani is the famous example.
The N64 prototype that became Super Smash Bros.; it had no special moves, dodges or items but already used Smash's rules. Iwata programmed it.

term: Draw the light, not the asset
meaning: His most common note to background artists: an asset isn't finished when it's modeled and textured with base colors; it must express the light it reflects in its environment.
Nested window hierarchies needed by feature-packed games like his own; he calls organizing them a constant struggle.
How far apart options are allowed to be; he wants it pushed as far as possible.
A circle where your views keep being reinforced by agreement, hiding the many people who disagree; it distorts how you judge design ideas, reviews and balance.
A status tier for top players that also matches them against each other.
Introducing new bugs while fixing one, the reason fixes and patches cannot ship instantly.
Xevious's predefined spawn order that advances as you play and can be rewound by destroying a specific enemy.
Stretches where the story sends the player back and forth; mechanically just a few flags, so their packaging (rewards, small joys, route choice, quick exit, mystery) decides whether they're fun.
Super Smash Bros. Ultimate's core concept: bringing back every past fighter, feasible because the team and dev environment carried over.
Kirby Air Ride's aim of broadening how people play instead of encouraging one perfect method.
Extra sound chips in Famicom cartridges, or the Disk System's wave memory channel, that gave Japanese versions richer music; the NES lacked the pins for them.
His umbrella word for everything (visuals, audio, programming, parameters) that together makes a massless game world feel real.
Kid Icarus: Uprising's difficulty wager: spend hearts to raise Intensity (default 2.0, up to 9.0) for bigger rewards or lower it (0.0 is nearly invincible); failure spills hearts and eases the retry.
Smash's flashy announcement videos for new fighters, split into CG and gameplay segments; made official from Smash for 3DS/Wii U, 37 in all.
The finished frame after everything is drawn into the framebuffer and post-processed; on powerful hardware it matters more than any single model.
Brawl's per-character super move; it could have been a generic item, but each fighter got their own to boost individuality.
Smash Ultimate's zoomed stop on a match-deciding hit; Sakurai calls it an extension of stop effects, closer to boss stop.
A knockback value that ignores damage so the target always reacts the same way; used on the early hits of multi-hit moves like Mario's Super Jump Punch.
His term for making the screen or a character shine: a full-screen flash for impact, a character flash to emphasize a change in status.
Sakurai's name for reading how fast the analog stick reaches the edge of its range to trigger a dash (localized as 'Tap' in the N64 Super Smash Bros.).
The Smash team's internal name for mirroring poses and movements when a character changes facing, so they face the camera from both sides.
The motion after the attack, when the character is briefly vulnerable (the recovery period); it takes the most screen time and determines the attack's impact.
One redraw of the screen and games' usual unit of time; at 60 fps, one second is 60 frames, and distance equals time times speed.
Sakurai's framing of post-launch balance and quality-of-life updates: welcome extras beyond the promise kept at launch, unlike fixes for fatal bugs.
Sources of fun other than push and pull: control feel, story, licensed fandom, simulation, building and crafting, rhythm.
Sakurai's name for a game's push and pull, or risk and reward: the fun of managing risks to get rewards. He calls it one part of a game's identity, not the whole.
Genre conventions taken for granted; he re-examines them at the start of each project.
Smash Ultimate's rank, where higher is better, measured against the whole player count, and the top player is hidden.
A per-attack minimum launch so even a barely damaged target reacts; paired with knockback scaling to keep it from inflating launches.
Any system or setting that evens out unequal players, from catch-up items to per-player difficulty.
His phrase for the controls and conventions that connect player and game; standard controls make it a little warmer.
A short description of the highlighted menu item, often at the bottom of the screen; his rule is never to explain an item using its own name.
Kirby Super Star's co-op system: an enemy's ability becomes a second playable character in a supporting role, with the camera following only the lead player.
Kirby Super Star's co-op solution: the camera follows the lead player, and a supporting Helper who drifts too far off screen 'Space Jumps' back.
A collapsible, folder-like text outline (heading, subheading, detail) he uses for ideas and specs, e.g. fighter, then special moves, then each move's spec.
Sakurai's name for the visual flair shown when an attack connects (sparks, flashes, shockwaves); guard effects count as hit marks too.
A brief stop of both attacker and target when an attack lands; whether it's there completely changes how heavy a hit feels. In Smash it always includes some shake.
One official place, usually the game's website, that delivers all of a game's information alongside social media.
Information overlaid on the play area, named after fighter-plane displays that let pilots read data without looking away; in games, everything placed at the forefront of the screen.
Easing off by hand, like letting a child grab the Smash Ball; possibly the most effective handicap there is.
The best version of a design, written first; you then course-correct from it for cost-effectiveness instead of bending the proposal out of shape up front.
A few pieces of art by an exceptional artist showing a game's world, scenery, characters and items, used as the reference that unifies the team's style.
A fighter's distinct identity; protecting it is the main reason he steps into balance decisions.
How many inputs per second the game demands; Brawl lowered speed partly because the higher the input density, the more online frame skips stood out.

Sakurai's name for the creative force that builds when you keep an idea to yourself; talking or posting about it releases the pressure and the idea loses power, so he writes the first draft before sharing a word.
Filling the gaps between key poses automatically; convenient, but it can overpower the key poses and make an animation feel slow.
A clicky scroll wheel Sakurai repeatedly proposed for controllers since the GameCube era so players could zip through menu choices.
Japanese comics technique of writing sound effects into the art; cited as inspiration for expressive text effects.
The Japanese word for a film director; whether a company calls the game director "director" or "kantoku" comes down to company culture.
Showing how far the player has come and how far is left to the next reward.
An in-game button settings screen for reassigning actions; Sakurai wants one in every game, however simple.
The crucial poses of an animation, which should be reached quickly rather than buried under interpolated in-betweens.
A per-attack factor that adjusts launch distance independently of damage, so a strong move can launch little or a weak move far.
The internal file-name class every action has in Smash, such as Attack11, AttackS4, AttackAirF or SpecialHi.
The rule that every tester uses the newest build, because bugs found on the wrong version aren't helpful and can cause problems.
Meteos' core action: matched blocks ignite and blast off into space instead of vanishing, which allows secondary ignitions and air docking.
The pose between the button press and the attack, also called anticipation or windup; in Sakurai's games it often jumps to a big pose on the very first frame.
His image for a game's concept: a beam you keep steering toward through the storm of development; change course and you get lost.
Swapping in lower-polygon models as objects move away from the camera; labor-intensive, so only worth it when the gain justifies it.
Where a looping track jumps back to; for Smash arrangements it can sit before or after the intro, with only a little looping within a match.
The part of a song players remember and hum; he insists arrangements keep it, and defines it by what players heard in play rather than by music theory.
His split between what players actually see and what they do not, used to allocate performance and labor.
A boss or encounter with one carefully crafted solution, which he calls 'almost like a tutorial'; a valid approach, set against free-form fights.
Comic symbols such as a bead of sweat or a vein mark that do not occur in real life but clearly signal an emotion.
Studying trends in audiences; Sakurai warns it describes paths already taken and shouldn't generate new game ideas.
Finishing and submitting the final version of a game; Sakurai notes it often leaves the team feeling bruised rather than triumphant, and online updates have taken away its sense of closure.
Finishing the final version of a game; Sakurai notes it often feels more wounding than triumphant because of the cuts it took, so he thanks the staff.
The line where fighters stand in a side-view game; an attack whose range doesn't cross it is hard to land.
His description of game worlds from a creator's view: decoration without mass or collision until gameplay and programming give it substance.
His analogy for difficulty: a good curve has peaks and flat stretches, not a constant incline.
His analogy for difficulty curves: a constant incline is just work, so build peaks (bosses that need a strategy) and flat stretches (empty areas, places to rack up gains).
Sakurai's presentation videos for Smash Ultimate DLC, in which he explains and plays each fighter himself; he counts them as marketing.
Sakurai's view that the success of development and of marketing are proportional to each other; also 'two wheels on one axle'.
The beetles of Kouchuu Ouja Mushiking, whose arcade battles used rock-paper-scissors with each Mushi specializing in one shape.
Brawl's feature offering several songs per game world and letting players choose, because each generation has its own version of a series.
Smash label modifiers for neutral, up, side, down and aerial.
The Space Invaders state where cannon and invader are far apart and neither attack can land.
Kirby Super Star's format: a collection of short, self-contained scenarios, each its own game with its own rules and theme, chosen from a cork board.
Enough depth in a beginner game's controls that advanced players enjoy it too.
An open board where any team member can post thoughts on how development is going; the director replies or routes items to teams.
A board where any team member can post opinions, suggestions and requests about how development is going; the director replies or forwards items to the right team.
The counter-force every motion needs to feel complete, such as falling for flight or slowdowns for speed.
The speed unit Sakurai used in specs for sprite games: how many pixels an object moves each frame.
Tunable values kept separate from code so designers can adjust them; "the code is the bones, and the parameters are the muscles."
A cooperative team relationship where someone who is stuck reports it early so the work can quickly be handed off, re-scoped or solved another way.
Distinct strengths and weaknesses for every option, which Sakurai protects when balancing.
A small set of real pieces made at final quality to test whether a project can be done and to win partners; for the channel, three episodes (C03, C11, D03).
An alternative written into a proposal ('or we could do this') that leaves the decision to someone else. Sakurai says to ditch it entirely in proposals.

The role that turns the director's ideas into spec sheets detailed enough to program from, and also balances gameplay, manages teams and supervises testing; on his later games, planners tuned the parameters.
Play testers keep playing to judge balance and tuning and report to planning; bug testers find and document reproducible bugs that a manager routes to the right team.

term: Playing what you want, how you want
meaning: The Smash philosophy that began with configurable rules: chaotic four-player battles with items, or tense one-on-one without.
An effect 'pops' when it has impact and contrast against any background, achieved with crisp shapes and dark elements rather than additive brightness alone.
The version of a sound effect the sound team submits for his review before revision; for impacts it typically has a longer tail than the final.
How much an environment object means to the player, which comes from gameplay (cautious, high-death play makes players scrutinize everything) rather than from the art alone.
The annual omnibus game-music concert Sakurai presided over for ten years from 2006, with the performance kept at the center.
The RPG exploration choice between going deeper for better spoils and getting out while you still can.
The stage after animatics where CG starts being woven in; Sakurai notes the line between the two is blurry.
The trade-off in licensed games, where faithfulness to the source comes first and you never get a perfect score on all fronts.
Sessions every few months where each team (graphics, sound, animation, effects, UI and so on) presents its work to everyone, so nobody feels like a cog in a machine.
The Famicom's crisp, castle-parapet-shaped waveform that carried most of its music; changing its time ratio (duty cycle) changes the texture.
The back-and-forth of taking risks to get rewards; used interchangeably with game essence.
The built-in reaction delay that stops Smash Ultimate CPUs from reacting faster than a human.
Where a fixed bug ticket goes instead of being deleted, in case the bug comes back.
A quick paintover of a team member's image (about five to ten minutes, done with a mouse) that shows the change he wants; an example of direction, not final art.
When a person's edits vanish and a file returns to its pre-edit state; common despite file-management tools.
The fixed email subject his team uses to ask for a review; requests are handled first come, first served and answered the same day.
Lighting that looks like it shines from behind a character, emphasizing the outline; Smash Ultimate uses it for certain damage types and statuses such as invulnerability.
Danger and opportunity as two sides of the same coin; they must be in close proximity and in the right amounts.
The part of a CRT image guaranteed to be visible (about 490 of 525 NTSC scanlines); developers assumed the edges were never seen.
The per-refresh signal his NES and SNES games used as their unit of time, which made PAL versions run at 5/6 speed.

term: screen shake patterns (large, medium, small, extra-small)
meaning: Smash's set of distinct shake patterns, not scaled copies: small is vertical only, medium adds horizontal, large shakes more.
A daily development screenshot shared with the team, which became his public daily screens on Twitter.
Whether an object or effect reads at its intended size; CG objects tend to look like scale models, and big things looking too small is the usual failure.
The players' guide website Sakurai built to explain Smash's push and pull when magazines ignored it; later updated every weekday for Brawl.
A quick flick of the analog stick combined with a button to trigger a stronger attack (or a jump) in Super Smash Bros.
Reading how fast the analog stick reaches its edge so a quick flick triggers a stronger attack, a jump or a dash.
Japanese for 'news flash' or 'breaking news'; added to the Dojo's name for Melee, when it posted screenshots and news during development.
From 'The Power of Suggestion': motivate yourself by imagining a deadline or threat closing in rather than a goal you'll reach eventually.
The audio lead who translates a director's notes into musical terms; Sakurai routes all arrangement feedback through Smash Ultimate's sound director.
All the layers of sound in a scene (wind in leaves, feet on dirt, clinking armor), each of which needs its own appropriate presence.
In Kirby Super Star, how a Helper who falls too far off-screen warps back to the lead player.
A mid-development change to the planned specification that scraps finished work. Sometimes unavoidable; the kind to avoid is one forced because the game isn't fun.
The planner's or director's blueprint for how something should be built and programmed; for a Smash fighter it includes an animation list and 70-80 pages of posed-figure images.
Ultimate's replacement for Trophies and a Subspace-style story: characters earned in battles recreating their source games, gathered into one story mode.
Scaling an object to flatten and elongate it for texture and life, always keeping its mass roughly the same.
Applying heavy stress, then suddenly setting the player free; also used for charging during a risky drift and releasing for a speed burst.
The ground or aerial resting pose every other animation starts from; Sakurai nails these down first and doesn't change them.
Open a game with a dramatic scene the player controls and explain how things got there later, instead of starting with backstory.
Game essence seen from the player side: how players manage risks to get rewards, or how they minimize losses and maximize gains, sometimes taking a bigger loss for an even bigger gain.
The four-step loop behind most games: an obstacle, its removal, a reward that strengthens you, and the next obstacle becoming easier.

Sakurai's policy for impact sounds: reach a strong level almost instantly (a short attack peaking at the start) and keep the reverberation short, so hits register right away and don't bury the next one.
Brawl's adventure mode with cutscenes, a story, a map and sticker power-ups, meant to give every character a moment in the spotlight; it needed its own movement parameters per fighter.
People who mostly play simple mobile games and may find even Kirby's Dream Land too hard; he suspects they are a very large opportunity.
In Sakurai's words, "charting the creative course": reviewing nearly every part of the team's work and requesting changes, while the creators do the work of reaching release quality.
Fully synchronous online play like Smash needs nearby players; asynchronous play like Mario Kart tolerates distance better.
The studio button a director uses to speak to voice actors in the booth; he usually directs Smash voice sessions this way.
Being specific about who you sell to, usually by age, gender and tastes; Sakurai prefers targeting by experience level such as 'beginners'.
Beats per minute: one clap per second is 60 BPM, two is 120. He treats tempo as a design decision for every scene.

term: Ten people produce seven people's work
meaning: His rule of thumb that management overhead means a ten-person team generally produces about seven people's worth of work, with more overhead as teams grow.
Sakurai's framing for Smash for 3DS (a handheld, one player per screen) versus Wii U (a console gathering many players), used to give each version its own modes.

term: The market is the best bug tester
meaning: After launch, so many players run the game that even one-in-a-thousand bugs surface and get uploaded, far beyond what internal testing can reach.

term: The original piece is always right
meaning: His rule for arranging beloved game music: the song as heard when playing the original game is the authority, quirks and hardware-driven structure included.
The thrill of barely scraping past a hazard, such as flying under a bridge.
A server-tracked task passed from person to person; whoever holds it is responsible for the work, and it carries a status and usually a deadline. Bugs are tickets too.
The lowest analog-stick tilt value that registers; it has to be configured for each console's stick.
A game's overall atmosphere, which should decide how much color and what style the UI uses.
Sakurai's rule for attack animation and expressions: on a small screen, and with CG losing information, exaggeration is the correct amount.
A character's root position; changing stance on hit can move it and push the target out of the rest of a combo.
In Sakurai's attack specs, the time until the attack can be canceled; with the attack start frame it bounds the lead-in and follow-through.
Space Harrier's opening period in which you can die as much as you want; many arcades left it on.
The director's job of cutting excess and offloading 'heavy or flammable cargo' when plans slip, to get the project back on course.
Melee's collectible figures with background info, which brought characters from across Nintendo's history in without making them playable; costly to produce.
Sakurai's tree metaphor for tastes: broad and shared when young (the trunk, the widest market), narrowing into niche branches with age.
Sakurai's image for menus: when a player pulls a menu open, things should be organized sensibly. How much is crammed into the drawers varies by game.
Sakurai's phrase for deliberately pushing a game in your own distinctive direction instead of letting others sway it toward the ordinary.
The idea that a score means more when expressed in a fitting unit, such as Brain Age, Crash Dollars or a power rating.

term: Up is down, and down is up
meaning: A leader's instructions flow downstream, but they are really requests made from the bottom up to the people who do the work, so nobody is above anyone.
Scrolling a texture's coordinates to animate a pattern; Smash's HUD uses upward-scrolling patterns behind fighter portraits to suggest burning spirit.
A parameter framework that changes character stats, used for party modes and customization but not level-playing-field matches.
Drawing fewer frames when the processor can't keep up; not the same as slowdown, where the game itself runs slower.
Dropping frames means redrawing less often; slowdown means the game itself runs slower. They are not the same.
Space Invaders' endgame state where invaders at the bottom can't hit the cannon: ultimate risk, ultimate reward, probably a bug.
Sakurai's description of himself: a freelance director with a near-staffless company (Sora Ltd.) who works on-site at partner studios one project at a time.
How 'light' or 'heavy' the same physical button feels, set by on-screen response: movement speed, inertia, jump physics, lag and frame rate.
The nesting of menu windows and submenus; one of his key design points for every menu, along with visual guidance, element size, brightness and saturation, and typeface.
A full-screen transition; usually a plain fade, but better when themed to the game and kept at an acceptable speed.
The Kirby team's name for Shotzo's shots, which slide around in a six-frame loop as they fly instead of moving in a straight line.
